04 · Read & review

The transcript

0:00 / 0:00

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Helen Ward's second call arrived forty-eight hours after her first meeting with Emma. She had spoken to the cousin whose 2011 travel application she had helped prepare. The cousin declined an interview, but had authorised Helen to show a copy of a decision letter with identifying details obscured. The permission was explicitly limited to inspection: no reproduction, recording or publication had been agreed.

Emma confirmed the terms before examining anything. Sarah entered the meeting room only with Helen's consent. Helen unfolded a photocopy bearing the Glenarraidh Education Trust's letterhead and a printed date in September 2011. Its appearance was consistent with the material Emma had seen elsewhere, but consistency of presentation was not authentication. Provenance and completeness remained unresolved.

The central sentence described the application as having been selected for travel support. A subsequent paragraph made any payment contingent upon documentary confirmation of enrolment and final travel expenditure. That distinction mattered. It identified an administrative decision in the language of the scheme, not evidence that an award had been disbursed.

“So we can add a beneficiary to our list,” Sarah said.

“Only if by beneficiary you mean someone described as selected in a copy we have not authenticated,” Emma replied. “It tells us nothing conclusive about payment.”

The same page included the fourteen-day review wording for unsuccessful applicants. Emma recognised its resemblance to the unused model notice Fiona Bell had obtained. If the copy was genuine, it would demonstrate that the template's language appeared in at least one individual letter. It would not prove that every applicant received comparable information, nor that those rejected could exercise their right effectively.

Emma asked the most important chronological question: when had the letter arrived? Helen could not say. Her direct memory concerned helping complete the application; she had encountered the letter again years later among family records. A printed date and a date of receipt were different propositions, especially when receipt supposedly triggered an appeal period.

Helen knew of no formal appeal involving her cousin and had no first-hand information about other students. Emma did not ask her to speculate about their outcomes or supply their names. She noted the conditions of the conversation, abstained from photographing the copy, and distinguished what she had personally read from what Helen recollected.

Before leaving, Helen agreed to seek further permission from her cousin for a redacted copy to be examined and verified. She did not commit to obtaining it. Emma neither pressed for the original nor treated consent to display as consent to publication.

Back at the newsroom, the September announcement and its later correction lay beside her notes. One apparently individual selection notice could not validate the reported figure of eight, much less resolve the absence of a corrected total. Even its conditional payment paragraph reinforced the distinction between a decision and a transaction.

Emma wrote two lines: Selection recorded in an unverified copy; payment not evidenced. She now had a more concrete lead than an archive heading, but the temptation to promote it into proof of the whole scheme had to be resisted.
